When are tasks acknowledged?
data.body:
When are Huey tasks acknowledged? In comparison with Celery, it has a `task_acks_late` to only acknowledge a task after it has been executed.

Sorry if this covered by the docs, I couldn't find anything.

data.author: coleifer
data.body:
Huey doesn't use an amqp-style workflow, nor does it attempt to ensure at-least-once delivery. There's no ack. The workflow, once a worker begins a task, is simple:

* Execute task
* If unhandled exception occurs and the task has one or more retries, it is re-enqueued.
* If the task finishes successfully, the return value is placed in the result store (though None return values are not stored by default).

data.title: Automatically consume an unfinished task if the Huey consumer is restarted
data.body:
Our Huey consumer restarts sometimes (it can be planned or unplanned maintenance, version upgrade, etc.).

Whenever this happens, tasks that are in the middle of consumption are "lost" and won't be retied.

Is it possible to add a mark in the Redis queue only after a task was completed (either successfully or unsuccessfully) so that if Huey is restarted the same task is picked up once more?

data.author: coleifer
data.body:
Huey is not guaranteed at-least-once delivery, and does not do acknowledgement of completed tasks. The consumer supports a soft shutdown for this reason -- any in-flight tasks will be finished before the consumer exits. It sounds like you are not using this, however.

You can add a signal handler for the `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` signal, which is run when a task is interrupted during execution (by a hard shutdown) - using this signal you can add logic to handle tasks that are interrupted during execution:

https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/signals.html

data.author: rudyryk
data.body: @coleifer I found this discussion and your recommendation useful and worth adding to documentation, some minimal example would be awesome. I believe it's quite common to restart workers on deployment to reload tasks code, and sometimes tasks are just too long, i.e. video processing etc.

data.author: coleifer
data.body:
3e7bdf253a02813eff138a2db6b00554d81a8e57 - hopefully this helps clarify.

Docs here: https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/consumer.html#consumer-shutdown

data.title: Retry Tasks on SIGTERM?
data.body:
Saw the following in the docs and having a bit of trouble interpreting it:
> Warning Huey does not guarantee at-least-once delivery of messages, and does not do acknowledgement of completed tasks. This means that if you terminate the consumer without letting it finish any currently-executing tasks, those tasks will be lost. To be alerted when this occurs, you can use Huey’s [Signals](https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/signals.html#signals) (specifically signals.SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED). The consumer will emit this for tasks that are interrupted during execution.

Let's say I send a SIGTERM signal to a consumer, and I have multiple consumers running (in a distributed fashion). Is there a way I can ensure this task will be added back to the queue and retried by another consumer?

data.author: raunakdoesdev

data.title: How to create a dead-letter-queue for tasks that can't be executed?
data.body:
Hey, I've been having fun where sometime we run into a task that's scheduled but which can't be run.

As an example of how this can happen, suppose that you schedule a task to persistent storage but then delete the code that would actually run it and restart the Huey workers.  Now there's a scheduled task that can't run and which will throw an exception when it gets to here.  It'll also stay on the queue, which means the scheduler will keep trying to rerun it. 
https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/master/huey/registry.py#L49

(Other ways this could happen include things like a bad custom serializer/deserializer, etc.)

What's the right way to catch errors such as this and make sure that tasks which're in that state don't stay queued?

If it's of any use, I'm happy to send a patch for [api.py:deserialize_task()](https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/master/huey/api.py#L299) to add a callback for if a task can't be deserialized?  That way people could decide what to do with it themselves?

data.author: coleifer
data.body:
>Now there's a scheduled task that can't run and which will throw an exception when it gets to here. It'll also stay on the queue, which means the scheduler will keep trying to rerun it.

What do you mean the scheduler will keep trying to rerun it? If the task was not found, then the scheduler just throws it out. It's easy to demonstrate this and verify for yourself. When the scheduler attempts to run the task that no longer exists/can't be executed, it will throw something like `huey.exceptions.HueyException: tasks.will_be_gone not found in TaskRegistry` and the task is discarded. It no longer remains in the schedule or the queue at that point.

If you want to catch these yourself you can just subclass `RedisHuey` or whatever and implement your own `deserialize_task()` that does what you want with the message.

data.author: p-j-l
data.body:
Thanks for the incredibly fast response!  My apologies, I was wrong there in thinking that the scheduler kept those on the queue.

Just to make sure that I understand: if I subclass RedisHuey I'll be able to catch errors in deserialization but not if the task doesn't exist in the registry?  Oh, I suppose I could add a custom check in the deserialize_task() call to see if the task name is in the registry before create_task() is called?

data.author: coleifer
data.body: No that's incorrect - you *will* be able to catch those errors inside `deserialize_task()`.

data.author: p-j-l
data.body: Sorry, one last quick question - when the scheduler gets the next batch of tasks to work though, what happens if just one of those were to have the sort of problems mentioned above?  Would just that task be thrown out?  Or would the entire batch be removed?

data.author: coleifer
data.body:
~~It would hardly be robust if the whole batch was removed... Only the problematic task is removed.~~

Hold up, let me make absolutely sure about this, you may have a good point and I missed something!

data.author: coleifer
data.body: You were absolutely right -- if a bad task was mixed in a batch of tasks that were ready to transition from the schedule -> main queue, then that whole batch of tasks would be lost! This is now fixed - the tasks are deserialized individually when reading the schedule and an exception is logged if one or more of them fails.

data.author: p-j-l
data.body: Much appreciated, thank you!

data.author: p-j-l

(On a side note, I'm happy to contribute some of my work engineering time to help with Huey if there's ever anything you'd like a hand with.  We make use of Huey so I feel like we should pay some of that back.)

data.title: Potential loss of due SQLite scheduled tasks when enqueue fails after schedule removal
data.body:
# Draft GitHub issue — Huey 3.4.0

## Title
Potential loss of due SQLite scheduled tasks when enqueue fails after schedule removal

## Body
Hi — I found what looks like a reliability gap in Huey 3.4.0's SQLite scheduled-work transfer path.

### Suspected sequence

In the inspected SQLite path, due scheduled rows are removed by the schedule read/dequeue operation, then the scheduler enqueues the returned tasks individually. If an enqueue raises after removal but before every task has been inserted into the task queue, the remaining due tasks may no longer be present in either the schedule table or the queue.

### Controlled source-slice fixture

I ran a local SQLite source-slice fixture against digest-pinned Huey 3.4.0 `storage.py` / `consumer.py` inputs. The fixture uses 503 due tasks (including the apparent 500-record deletion boundary), a future scheduled task, and a task in another queue.

| injected enqueue failure point | queued due tasks after reopen | missing due tasks |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| none (control) | 503 | 0 |
| before first enqueue | 0 | 503 |
| after one enqueue | 1 | 502 |
| after 500 enqueues | 500 | 3 |

The future scheduled task and the other-queue records remained intact in these fixture cases.

### Scope / limitations

This is **not** a claim about security, data durability under power loss, concurrency, or all Huey backends. It is a bounded SQLite/source-slice result with injected enqueue failures. I have not yet run a whole-package production configuration or real process-crash reproduction, so I am reporting this as a potential correctness/recovery issue rather than a confirmed production defect.

### Question

Is loss of unqueued due scheduled tasks after an enqueue exception intentional? If not, would an atomic transfer / recovery-marker approach be appropriate, so a failed transfer leaves scheduled rows retryable rather than deleting them before all queue inserts succeed?

I can provide the small standalone fixture and the exact source hashes if that would help maintainers reproduce or assess this.

data.author: novahoshino
data.body:
Runnable standalone source-slice reproducer:
https://gist.github.com/novahoshino/877eff4b4e49eff828e8a359a9fdad74

From a checkout of Huey tag `3.4.0`:

```bash
python3 reproduce_scheduled_enqueue_loss.py
```

It verifies the inspected source hashes before exercising the SQLite schedule-read / enqueue sequence and prints the four control/failure cases.

As noted in the README, this remains a bounded source-slice fixture rather than a full-package or crash-durability reproduction.

data.author: coleifer
data.body: I mean...this is technically correct but it's been this way for years and is somewhat meh in my opinion. Fixed by wrapping the enqueue so a single failure is at least recoverable.
